title: Pick the right tool for each security symptom
purpose: Choose the right check for three security symptoms of a page (an old library, a missing CSP header, an extension that asks for every site) and put the checks in one quick order.
summary: A quick security pass on a page has three checks. Retire.js finds libraries with known vulnerabilities. The Content-Security-Policy response header shows which scripts the page allows. The match patterns and permissions of an extension show which pages its content scripts can read. Each deep dive shows the result of a weak choice and of the right choice.
explanation: Each symptom needs the tool that can see it: a version needs a vulnerability database, a policy needs the response header, and access needs the extension manifest.

learning_check.question: A page loads an old copy of a JavaScript library. Which check tells you whether that version has known vulnerabilities?
learning_check.answer: Retire.js: it compares the library version with its list of versions that have known vulnerabilities.

slides.heading: Which tool sees this problem?
slides.notes: State the task: three symptoms, three tools, and one short order for a security pass.

visual.subtitle: A quick security pass in three checks

slides.heading: Three symptoms on one page
slides.notes: Each symptom is a different kind of fact: a version, a response header, and a permission in a manifest.

items: The page loads an old library version
The response has no CSP header
A helper extension asks for all sites

slides.heading: Pick a symptom, then a tool
slides.notes: Open one deep dive per symptom. Each shows a weak choice, its result, and the right check. Back returns here.

slides.heading: Order the quick pass
slides.notes: Start with what the page loads, then what the page allows, then what your own tools can read.

slides.heading: Match the tool to the fact
slides.notes: A wrong tool gives a calm answer to the wrong question. Ask what kind of fact the symptom is, then pick the tool that reads it.

slides.heading: Weak choice: read the version by eye
slides.notes: The Elements panel shows the script tag and maybe a version, but not which versions have known vulnerabilities.

visual.verdict: Use a scanner that knows the vulnerable versions.

slides.heading: Right choice: scan with Retire.js
slides.notes: Retire.js detects JavaScript libraries and reports versions with known vulnerabilities. It runs as a command line tool and inside Burp Suite and OWASP ZAP.

items: Retire.js finds the library and version
It checks its list of vulnerable versions

slides.heading: Where the policy comes from
slides.notes: The server sends the policy in the Content-Security-Policy response header. A meta element can also set a policy, but it lacks some features.

slides.heading: Allowlist or strict policy
slides.notes: MDN recommends a strict policy with nonces or hashes for scripts, because an allowlist of hosts is hard to keep safe.

slides.heading: What host access gives a content script
slides.notes: The manifest match patterns choose the pages. A content script runs in each matching page and reads its DOM.

slides.heading: Right choice: read the access first
slides.notes: Access to all sites lets the content script read every page you open. activeTab gives access only after you invoke the extension.
